newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss, WJC meet on details of Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss, WJC meet on details of Holocaust fund.

text.p: Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti met a senior official of the World Jewish Congress (WJC) on Monday to work out details of a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors launched by Swiss banks.

Cotti met WJC secretary general Israel Singer in the Swiss capital Berne two weeks after the Swiss government and major Jewish groups agreed to put aside months of quarreling and cooperate in compensating Holocaust victims.

Singer's deputy, assistant secretary general Maram Stern, told reporters both sides were trying to reach agreement quickly on who would control the fund's purse strings and how to decide which victims of the Holocuast would benefit.
"Our common denominator is that we want to decide efficiently and quickly on the structure of the fund," Stern said.

The WJC delegation will meet Swiss officials again on Tuesday and be joined by representatives of Swiss banks, other companies who have said they want to pay into the fund and gypsies, who also want compensation for mass persecution by the Nazis.

The WJC has led a campaign since 1995 demanding compensation from Switzerland along two lines -- from Swiss banks for keeping the accounts of Jews killed in the Holocaust and from the country as a whole for profiting cynically from business with Nazi Germany.
Singer said earlier the WJC, which for months had hammered the Swiss with critcism, now wanted to cooperate after Swiss banks and the government agreed to set up the humanitarian fund.
"There are no problems. We have engaged ourselves in a process and we trust and hope this process will bear fruit and continue to develop and grow," he told Swiss radio.

The Swiss government, which at the start of the year said it would never establish such a fund, announced two weeks ago that it would take over a private 100 million Swiss franc ($69 million) set up by the country's three biggest banks and work with the WJC and Swiss Jews to set up a mechanism for its "timely distribution".

Sources close to the negotiations have said they expect a foundation to be set up to administer payments and give priority to the neediest survivors and those who never received any compensation, such as the Jews of Eastern Europe.
